messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thanh was sixty years old, a hotel manager in a mid-sized city, when he finally sat in a clinician’s office. For thirty-two years he had worked in the same industry, rising from front-desk clerk to overseeing a full staff, and for thirty-two years he had prided himself on his composure. That composure had shattered on a Tuesday afternoon three years ago, during what should have been a routine inspection of a newly delivered cleaning solvent. A valve on the storage drum had been improperly sealed, and when Thanh leaned in to check the label, a plume of caustic vapor shot directly into his face. The taste—acrid, metallic, chemical—filled his mouth and throat instantly. He remembered staggering backward, gasping, certain he was dying, his lungs seizing as the burn spread down into his chest. He was rushed to the emergency room, treated for chemical inhalation, and released after six hours. Medically, he was fine. But something in him had not come home from that hospital.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that taste began to intrude without warning. Thanh would be standing at the front desk, reviewing a reservation, and suddenly the acrid flavor would flood his mouth, and with it came the full sensation of the vapor—the heat, the panic, the certainty that he was about to stop breathing. He would feel his heart race, his palms sweat, and for a few terrible seconds he was back in that storage room. The memory forced its way in, unwanted, and he could not push it away. He began to notice that his body felt constantly tense, braced for something, his muscles tight even when he was sitting still. He started scanning the hallways of his hotel for anything unusual—a strange smell, a loose pipe, a canister left in the open. He checked his own body, too, pressing on his chest, feeling his pulse, looking for any sign that something was wrong. The checking itself seemed to make the memories come back more sharply, as if the vigilance invited the taste to return.

Thanh had come to believe something fundamental about himself: that he could not stop bad things from happening. He had always been a careful man, a planner, someone who anticipated problems before they arose. But the accident had happened anyway, and he had been powerless. That helplessness settled into his bones. He began to feel that he no longer belonged anywhere—not at work, where the cleaning supply closet now felt like a trap, and not at home, where his partner could not understand why he flinched at the smell of bleach. His own body, which he had always trusted, now felt like a source of betrayal. He could not trust it to stay calm, could not trust it not to react as if danger were present when nothing was actually wrong. When a delivery was late, he assumed something catastrophic had happened. When a guest complained about a strange odor in the hallway, his chest tightened and he had to excuse himself.

The helplessness drove him to monitor his surroundings obsessively. The more he scanned, the more he found reasons to be alert—a faint chemical smell from a distant floor, a bottle left unlabeled in a storage room. Each discovery confirmed that danger was everywhere, that he could not let his guard down. And each wave of hypervigilance seemed to trigger the memory again, the taste rising in his throat, the reliving of that moment when his lungs seized. The reliving, in turn, reinforced his belief that his body was unreliable, that he was always one wrong breath away from disaster. The loop tightened. He began avoiding conversations where the event might come up, steering colleagues away from any mention of chemicals or accidents. When a staff member asked about the new solvent protocol, Thanh changed the subject and walked away quickly, his heart pounding.

His partner noticed that he had stopped cooking at home, because the smell of onions and oil sometimes reminded him of something acrid, and he could not separate the two. He stopped going to the hardware store, because the cleaning aisle made him dizzy. His world had narrowed. At work, he still managed, but he had started delegating the supply inventory to an assistant, claiming he was too busy. He was not too busy. He was afraid. What frightened him most was the feeling that the memory was not a memory—it was happening right now, every time. He could taste it. He could feel it. And he was certain that if he relaxed, if he stopped checking, if he let his guard down for even a moment, the next exposure would kill him.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a panic attack in the hotel lobby last month. A guest had dropped a glass bottle of cologne near the front desk, and the sharp, alcohol-based scent hit Thanh from across the room. He had frozen, then bolted to the bathroom, where he stood over the sink, gasping, tasting the vapor from three years ago. His assistant manager found him there, pale and shaking. Thanh had been humiliated. He had always been the calm one, the one others relied on. Now he was afraid he would lose his job, his relationship, his sense of who he was. He came to therapy not entirely sure it would help, but certain that he could not go on like this. He hoped, more than anything, to stop tasting that chemical burn every time he tried to breathe.
